ch20.title: By the Charcoal Fire
ch20.b002: Peter walked well behind the others. Ahead of him, among the olive trees, the torches swayed and climbed along the slope of the hill, and he knew that somewhere in the middle of that moving light walked a man with his hands bound. He knew it, and yet the knowledge would not go into his body. Only a few hours before, in the upper room, those same hands had washed his feet. Only a little while ago the Master had been sitting in the moonlight beside the olive press. Now he was being led away like a robber taken on the road. Peter put one foot in front of the other and felt as though he were walking through a dream from which he could not wake.
ch20.b003: The procession did not go down into the city. It turned instead toward the palace of Annas, the former high priest, which stood on the slope of Mount Olivet not far from the garden of Gethsemane. High walls and a heavy gate loomed black against the night. The gate swung open and the torches were drawn inside, one after another, as if the house were swallowing them. From a distance Peter saw John going in beside the captain of the Roman soldiers, close enough to the Master to have touched him.
ch20.b004: When he came near the gate, Peter stopped. The sword still hung at his belt. He had drawn it in the garden, and at one word from the Master he had pushed it back into its sheath. That voice was still in his ears, telling him to put the blade away. He could not walk into that house with a sword on his hip. He unbuckled it and flung it into the brush beside the road. He heard a small sound as the iron struck a stone. His waist felt suddenly light, and it seemed to him that something else had gone out of him along with the weight of the sword.
ch20.b005: He stood before the gate with no way in. The woman who kept it peered at him through the gap, plainly suspicious. Then someone in the courtyard caught sight of him. It was John, who was on the point of following the Master into the house. John knew him at once, went over to the portress, and spoke a few words to her. She evidently knew John; she nodded and opened the gate a little wider, and was glad enough to do it.
ch20.b006: Peter stepped inside. By then John had already vanished into the inner rooms. Peter could feel the portress watching his back for a long moment as he crossed the yard.
ch20.b007: He did not know that a little earlier Judas Iscariot had also come up to this gate. Judas had looked in, seen Jesus and John standing in the courtyard, and turned away without entering. He knew that the real trial would be held later at the house of Caiaphas, and he went on there. It had happened only a short while before Peter reached the gate.
ch20.b009: There was a reason why no one barred John’s way in this palace. The Roman captain had given his word for him, but more than that, John and his brother James were familiar faces to the older servants of the house. Annas was a distant relative of their mother, Salome, and the two brothers had been guests there many times since their boyhood. In John’s memory the house was wide and cool, with marble floors that shone underfoot. Tonight the Master was dragged across those same floors with his hands tied.
ch20.b010: Annas sat in a large chair in his spacious audience chamber. He had grown rich on the revenues of the temple; he had set his son-in-law Caiaphas in the office of high priest; and with his ties to the Roman authorities there was no single man in all Jewry more powerful than he. He had Jesus brought to stand before him and studied him for some moments without a word. The two had not met for several years, not since the day the Master had called at this house and, finding himself coldly received, had promptly left. Annas had half hoped he might lean on that old acquaintance and persuade the Galilean to give up his claims and leave the country. But once they stood face to face, he knew the idea was hopeless. The man before him was even more composed and more majestic than he remembered.
ch20.b011: Annas told him that surely he understood something had to be done about his teaching, since it was disturbing the peace and order of the land. The Master looked straight into his eyes and gave no answer. Annas then asked for the names of his disciples, besides Simon Zelotes, the agitator. John held his breath. His own name might come from those lips next, or his brother’s, or Peter’s. The Master only looked down upon the old man and kept his silence.
ch20.b012: Annas’s face hardened. Did the prisoner not care, he asked, whether he had a friend in him or not? Had he no regard for the power Annas held over the outcome of the trial that was coming? Only then did the Master speak. He told Annas that he would have no power over him at all unless the Father permitted it. Some, he said, would destroy the Son of Man out of ignorance, not knowing any better; but Annas, his friend, knew very well what he was doing. How, then, could he turn away from the light of God?
ch20.b013: The voice was so kindly that Annas was almost bewildered by it, and so was John. Here was the Master calling the man who meant to judge him “friend,” just as he had called Judas in the garden.
ch20.b014: Annas gathered himself and asked what exactly he was trying to teach the people, and what he claimed to be. The Master answered that he had always spoken openly to the world. He had taught in the synagogues and many times in the temple, in the hearing of everyone, and nothing he had said had been said in secret. Why ask him, then? Let Annas send for those who had heard him and ask them.
ch20.b015: At that, the chief steward of the palace, who stood close by, struck the Master in the face with his open hand and demanded how he dared answer the high priest like that.
ch20.b016: The slap rang through the room. John’s body lurched forward of its own accord, and he barely managed to stop himself; his nails were biting into his palms. Annas said nothing to rebuke his servant. The Master turned and looked at the steward. He called him friend again, and asked him to bear witness to the evil if he had spoken evil; but if he had spoken the truth, why strike him? There was no anger in it, only the question. It was the steward who lowered his eyes first.
ch20.b017: Inwardly Annas regretted that the man had raised his hand, but he was too proud to say so. In his confusion he rose and went off into another room, and for almost an hour the Master was left alone among the household servants and the temple guards. John stood against the wall and kept watch through that hour. Not once did the Master turn to look at him. Yet John knew that he knew he was there. When Annas came back at last, he pressed the prisoner about whether he claimed to be the Messiah and got little for his pains, and soon messengers arrived from the palace of Caiaphas asking when the prisoner would be brought.
ch20.b019: A charcoal fire had been lit in the middle of the courtyard, for the night was chilly, and a few servants and guards stood around it warming their hands. Peter went toward it because there was nowhere else to put himself. He edged in among them and held both hands out over the coals. The charcoal glowed red. Now and then a spark leaped up, and the acrid smell of it stung his nose.
ch20.b020: He did not belong there. The Master had told John to keep near at hand, but he had told Peter no such thing. The apostles had been plainly warned not to throw their lives away during the days of the trial and the death. And here was Peter in the very midst of the Master’s enemies, warming himself at their fire. He did not think about any of that. He could not think properly about anything. He still could not take in that the Master had truly been arrested. Nor could he take in that he himself was standing in the courtyard of Annas, shoulder to shoulder with the servants of the high priest, getting warm. Where were the others now? And how had John got in? The servants here must know John, he decided; that would be why John had been able to ask the gatekeeper to let him in. That was as far as his thinking went.
ch20.b021: The woman who kept the gate came over to the fire. She looked into Peter’s face, and with a teasing note in her voice she said:
ch20.b022: “Aren’t you one of that man’s disciples too?”
ch20.b023: Peter ought not to have been startled. It was John who had asked her to let him through, so of course she would guess. But he was wound so tight that the question went through him like lightning. He had been found out. Only one thought filled him: to get out of this alive. The words were out before he had thought them, the way his words had always come.
ch20.b025: The woman shrugged and went back to her post. Peter kept his hands over the fire. They were trembling. It was the heat, he told himself. Around the fire the servants were muttering about the Galilean who had been brought in that night. One said he had seen the man the day he drove the traders out of the temple; another said the stories about his raising the dead were all idle talk. Someone laughed. Peter stood in the middle of that laughter and stared down into the coals. If he opened his mouth, he was afraid his Galilean speech would give him away.
ch20.b026: A little later another servant, who had been eyeing him, came up and asked whether he had not seen Peter in the garden when they took the fellow. Was he not one of his followers too? Now Peter was thoroughly frightened. He could see no way out. He denied it hard and flat: he did not know the man, and he was not one of his followers.
ch20.b027: Then the portress came again, and this time she drew him off to one side. She was sure, she said, that he was a disciple of this Jesus. Not only had one of the man’s followers asked her to let him in, but her sister, who was standing right there, had seen him with the man in the temple. Why did he keep denying it? Peter burst out cursing and swearing. He was no follower of that man, he said; he did not know him; he had never even heard of him.
ch20.b028: Never even heard of him. Even as the words left his mouth he did not grasp what he was saying. He was only getting away.
ch20.b029: He left the fire and wandered about the courtyard. He wanted to run, but running would draw every eye to him. The night wind crept in under his cloak, and when the cold had settled into him again he had no choice but to go back to the fire. As he stretched out his hands, the man beside him looked at him and said that he was surely one of the man’s disciples; this Jesus was a Galilean, and Peter’s own speech showed that he was a Galilean too. Once more Peter denied any connection with his Master.
ch20.b030: Galilean speech. The tongue he had grown up with on the shore at Bethsaida. And now that tongue was accusing him. He left the fire and climbed the steps to the porch, where he stood alone in the shadow of a pillar so that he would not have to face anyone.
ch20.b031: More than an hour passed there. He paced up and down the porch to keep warm, and in that time a strange thought took hold of him. He began to reflect on how cleverly he had dodged the servants’ questions. They had tried to tie him to Jesus, and each time he had slipped free. They had no right to question him anyway, neither moral nor legal; who were they, mere servants, to demand answers of him? So he owed them none. He had not been seized; he had not been thrown into prison. Peter, in the dark, actually congratulated himself. Well handled, he thought. He did not yet see how strange that thought was. A man who has taken the first wrong step finds it all too easy to keep walking and to call the road right.
ch20.b033: The gatekeeper and her sister happened to come along the porch and met him there. Half in fun, the two of them charged him again with being a follower of Jesus. Peter denied it again.
ch20.b034: The moment the words were out, the cock crowed.
ch20.b035: It tore through the darkness, high and long and piercing. Peter froze where he stood. He knew that sound. Every dawn at Bethsaida it had called him out to the nets. And over it now came the voice he had heard a few hours earlier in the upper room: before the cock crowed this very night, he would deny his Master three or four times.
ch20.b036: He tried to count, but the numbers slid through his fingers. Everything he had done fell on him at once. He had said no. He had said he did not know him. He had said he had never heard of him. And he had sworn and cursed to make it stick. Only now could he see what that earlier thought had been, the one in which he had praised himself for managing so well. Peter leaned against the pillar to stay upright. There was no strength left in his legs.
ch20.b037: Just then the doors of the palace opened. Torches came out. The guards were leading the Master away to the house of Caiaphas. The bound hands, the mark of the steward’s palm still on his face, the face of a man who had not slept all night. The Master passed in front of the porch, directly before the place where Peter stood.
ch20.b038: The Master stopped. He turned and looked at Peter.
ch20.b039: The torchlight fell full on Peter’s face. It was the face that had always been so sure of itself, the face that was always out in front, always calling out. The Master saw that it was full of despair. And he looked at it.
ch20.b040: Peter never forgot that look as long as he lived. There was no reproach in it. There was no disappointment, and none of the cold satisfaction of having been proved right. What was there was pity and love, so mingled that he could not tell where one ended and the other began. Had any man ever been looked at like that? It was not the look of someone gazing down at a man who has fallen; it was the look of someone still holding on to him after the fall. Peter could hide nothing before those eyes. Nor did he need to. The Master already knew everything. He knew it, and he looked at him that way all the same.
ch20.b041: A guard shoved the Master forward. He walked on. The torches moved off through the gate and away.
ch20.b042: Peter stumbled after them. Out through the gate, a few steps, a few more. Then he could go no farther. His knees gave way and he sat down by the side of the road, and he wept. He wept like a child, doubled over, unable to swallow the sound. A fisherman of thirty-four, the father of three children, the man with the loudest voice among the apostles, sat in the dirt of the road and wept bitterly.
ch20.b044: When the weeping had eased a little, Peter raised his head. Beyond the gate the red glow of the charcoal fire still flickered above the courtyard wall. And as he looked at it, another fire rose before his eyes.
ch20.b045: It was the garden of Zebedee’s house, on the night of their ordination, a little more than three years before. That January night had been cold, and the twins had gathered dry branches and built a small fire in the middle of the garden, and its light had turned twelve faces ruddy. The Master had told them that if what he asked was too hard, they could even now turn back. They had drawn apart under the trees to talk among themselves, and when they came back it was Peter who had spoken for them all. We will go on with you, he had said. Not one of us will turn back. We will drink the cup.
ch20.b046: His voice had shaken when he said it, but it had been loud and clear, and he had not doubted a word of it. His brother Andrew had laid a hand on his shoulder. The fire that night had been warm.
ch20.b047: One by one the faces around that fire came back to him. Thomas hugging his knees and muttering to himself; Simon Zelotes nodding with his jaw clenched; Nathaniel swallowing hard instead of making his usual joke; the twins sitting hand in hand. And Judas, the last of them to nod, the firelight falling on only half his face. Tonight Judas had handed the Master over. And Peter had said he did not know him. Peter could not see what difference there was between the two. The thought pressed him down into the earth.
ch20.b048: That fire had been warm and this one was cold. No, this fire had been warm as well. The charcoal he had held his hands over had warmed his body well enough. It was only that beside it he had said no. On that night, by a fire, he had sworn he would not turn back; tonight, by a fire, he had said he did not know him.
ch20.b049: It was a strange thing. A few hours ago in the garden he had drawn his sword. He had not given an inch before the soldiers with their torches or the armed guard. He might have died there, and he had not been afraid. Yet before a question a serving girl tossed at him half in jest, he had collapsed. The man who could stand up to a sword had fallen down before a laugh. Tonight, for the first time, he learned that he was that kind of man.
ch20.b050: The Master had known. In the upper room he had looked straight into Peter’s wet eyes and told him. Peter had not believed it; such a thing could not happen, he had thought. And the Master had said something more. He had asked what Peter would have to go through before he learned to set a guard upon his lips. And he had said that the experience Peter would pass through that very night would surely be a great help to him. Peter remembered it and wept again. Help? What help was there in this? And yet the Master had known all of it beforehand, and knowing it, he had spoken those words.
ch20.b051: Then another memory came. At Hippos, when Peter was in charge of the workers there, he had asked how many times he must forgive a brother who wronged him, and the Master had said not seven times only but seventy times and seven. Peter had never forgotten it. But he could not turn that word on himself now. It was a word about forgiving others, not about being forgiven. He could not believe that he could be forgiven. Only the look that had turned on him under the torches stayed lodged in the very center of his unbelief, and would not come out.
ch20.b052: As the sky began to grey, Peter got to his feet. He had to find his brother. He made his way, staggering, back to the camp near Gethsemane. The camp was deserted. The tents flapped in the dawn wind, and where the fires had been there was only ash. David Zebedee was there with three or four messengers, keeping the place. David looked at Peter’s face and asked him nothing. The other apostles had scattered, he said. Nathaniel, Matthew, Philip, and the twins had gone into hiding at Bethpage and Bethany; Thomas, James, and Simon Zelotes had hidden themselves in the city. Andrew was in Jerusalem, at the home of Nicodemus. David sent Peter there in the charge of one of his messengers.
ch20.b053: In an upstairs room in the house of Nicodemus, Andrew opened the door. He looked at his brother: the swollen eyes, the cloak caked with dirt, the waist where no sword hung. Andrew asked him nothing. He had always been that kind of brother. He simply stepped aside and made room for him to come in. Peter sank down in a corner, and Andrew sat beside him. For a long while neither of them said anything. His brother’s shoulder rested against his own, as it had beside the fire in the garden that night.
ch20.b055: At that hour John was in the palace of Caiaphas. At about half past three that Friday morning the high priest called the Sanhedrist court of inquiry to order. It was not the chamber of hewn stone in the temple but the high priest’s own house, and it was no regular meeting either. Only some thirty members had been summoned, those who had openly opposed the Master all along. On three earlier occasions the Sanhedrin had already resolved that he must die.
ch20.b056: The Master stood before the court in his ordinary clothes, his hands bound behind his back. A stir went through the room. They had never seen a prisoner like this. They had never seen a man on trial for his life stand so still.
ch20.b057: More than a score of false witnesses came forward one after another. Their stories contradicted each other, and the fabrication was so obvious that the councilors themselves were ashamed of it. The Master stood looking down on them with a kindly face, and that face alone was enough to make the liars stumble over their words. He answered none of them. At last two of them came close to agreeing: they said they had heard him say he would destroy this temple made with hands and in three days build another made without hands. John knew that saying. He knew too that when the Master spoke it he had pointed to his own body. But no one asked John anything.
ch20.b058: The high priest shouted at him: had he no answer to any of these charges? The Master did not open his mouth. That silence weighed more than any reply could have. Annas, who had arrived soon after the witnesses began, sat down beside Caiaphas, seized on the saying about the temple, and drew three charges out of it. They were words meant for Pilate’s ears.
ch20.b059: Caiaphas could bear it no longer. He rushed to the Master’s side, shook his finger in his face, and adjured him by the living God to say whether he was the Deliverer, the Son of God. The Master answered that he was. He said that soon he would go to the Father, and that before long the Son of Man would be clothed with power and would once more reign over the hosts of heaven.
ch20.b060: John heard that answer. The one who had said almost nothing all night had answered this question at once, and plainly. He had shown no interest in any other question put to him. Only when they asked who he was, and what he had come to do, did he say yes.
ch20.b061: The high priest tore his outer garments. What need had they of witnesses now, he cried; they had all heard the blasphemy; what did they think should be done? The voices in the room became one voice. He deserved to die; let him be crucified. Caiaphas stepped forward and struck the Master in the face. As the councilors filed out of the room they spat in his face, and one palm after another came down on his cheek. In that disorder, at half past four, the first session ended.
ch20.b062: The hour that followed was the darkest of all. The Master was left in the audience chamber in the hands of the temple guards and the high priest’s servants. They mocked him, spat on him, beat him. They struck his face with a rod and then told him to prophesy, since he was the Deliverer, and say who had hit him. When the abuse first began, the Master gave John a single nod. It meant: go. John understood. If he watched this, he would not be able to bear it. He would shout and throw himself at them, and then he too would die. The Master was preventing that. The one being beaten was protecting the one who watched.
ch20.b063: John withdrew into the next room. Through the wall came laughter and dull blows. He stood with his forehead pressed against the stone. He was alone and he was terrified. Where was his brother? Where was Peter? He was by himself. He thought of the upper room a few hours earlier: the Master on his knees with the basin, the hands that had cradled his feet. Those hands were bound now on the other side of this wall while men struck him. He had told them he was among them as one who serves, and men were treating that servant worse than a slave. Through the whole of that hour the Master said nothing at all.
ch20.b064: At half past five the court reassembled, and the Master was brought into the side room where John was waiting. John looked at his face. It was swollen, and the spittle had dried on it. But the eyes were the same. Only when he saw those eyes could John breathe again. In half an hour the court drew up its indictment for Pilate under three heads, without witnesses and without the prisoner present. Three Pharisees left rather than be part of that. Judas sat in that session too, but he gave no testimony.
ch20.b065: Meanwhile some of the women of the high priest’s household came with their friends to look at the strange prisoner. One of them asked him if he was the Messiah, the Son of God. He told her that if he said so she would not believe him, and if he asked her she would not answer.
ch20.b066: At six in the morning the Master was led out to Pilate. John went with him.
ch20.b068: The trial before Pilate was held on the steps in front of the praetorium, the governor’s quarters built onto the fortress of Antonia. The accusers stayed outside, unwilling to enter a gentile house where leaven might be found and so make themselves unclean on the day of preparation for the Passover. They were bent on putting a man to death, yet they would not cross a threshold that might defile them. John stood at the foot of the steps and saw it all. Among the fifty or so accusers was the face of Judas.
ch20.b069: Pilate asked what charge they brought. They named none; they said only that if the man were not an evildoer they would not have handed him over. Then, said Pilate, judge him by your own law. They answered that they were not permitted to put anyone to death. When Pilate insisted he would not examine the man until the charges were put in writing, the indictment in three heads was handed over at last. It was the first time the Master had heard it. He made no reply.
ch20.b070: John, at the foot of the steps, watched him standing there above his accusers. He was looking down on them, and there was no contempt in his face, only a real pity and a sorrowful affection. Pilate too was astonished at that silence. He took the Master and John inside and questioned the prisoner privately. He said he did not believe the first charge, and then asked whether Jesus had ever taught that tribute should be refused to Caesar. The Master pointed to John and told Pilate to ask him. John, his voice shaking, testified that the Master and his apostles paid taxes both to Caesar and to the temple. Pilate told John to let no one know he had spoken with him. John kept that promise all his life. What he heard in that room that day he never told, not even to his brother, not even to Peter.
ch20.b071: Pilate asked if he was the king of the Jews. The Master smiled at him and asked whether he was asking for himself or repeating what others had said. Then he told Pilate that his kingdom did not belong to this world; if it did, his disciples would be fighting for him. That he stood there in bonds was proof enough. He had come to bear witness to the truth, he said, and everyone who loved the truth heard his voice. Pilate, half mocking and half in earnest, asked what truth was, and who could know.
ch20.b072: John heard the question. Before the man who asked what truth was, the truth sat bound.
ch20.b073: Pilate went out and declared that he found no fault in the man. The accusers seethed. One of the councilors stepped up beside the governor and said the prisoner had been stirring up the people from Galilee all the way through Judea. At the word Galilee, Pilate saw a way to be rid of the decision, and he ordered the guards to take the prisoner to Herod.
ch20.b074: As they set off toward Herod’s palace, the Master turned to John. He told him there was nothing more John could do for him now; he was to go to his mother and bring her, so that she might see him before he died. John did not want to leave him alone among his enemies. All night he had been told to keep near, and now he was told to go. But he did not argue. He turned and ran for the Bethany road. He did not see what came after. For the rest of his life John would know the next three hours only from the mouths of others.
ch20.b075: No friend of the Master saw them. Those who loved him either had not yet heard of the night’s arrest or were in hiding; only his enemies and the easily led crowd stood before the praetorium that morning. Herod, who had long wanted to see him work some wonder, questioned him for a quarter of an hour and got not a single word. He mocked him, put an old purple royal robe on him, and sent him back to Pilate. Pilate told the accusers that neither he nor Herod had found anything worthy of death; he would chastise the man and let him go. Then a great crowd came surging up the steps to ask for the release of a prisoner at the Passover, and Pilate thought he had found his escape. But they were calling for Barabbas, an agitator taken in robbery and murder on the Jericho road, and when Pilate offered them the choice, the chief priests and councilors shouted for Barabbas first and the crowd took up the cry. It was the same city that had welcomed the Master with shouts only days before. A sealed note came from Pilate’s wife, Claudia, begging him to have nothing to do with that just and innocent man, for she had suffered much in a dream that night because of him. While Pilate stood over it and hesitated, the rulers moved through the crowd and worked on it, and when he asked again what he should do with the king of the Jews, they roared with one voice: Crucify him.
ch20.b076: Pilate made one last appeal to their pity. He had the Master scourged, a punishment the law allowed only for those already condemned to the cross. The soldiers crowned him with woven thorns, put the purple robe on him again, knelt in mockery, and struck him. Then Pilate led him out bleeding before the crowd and told them to behold the man. The crowd caught its breath for a moment, and then shouted louder and longer than before. When the high priest declared that by their law the man must die for making himself the Son of God, Pilate grew more afraid, and took him inside once more to ask who he really was. The Master told him he would have no power over him at all unless it had been allowed from above, and that those who had betrayed him and handed him over bore the greater sin. Pilate was on the point of letting him go when Caiaphas shook a finger in his face and said, for all to hear, that if he released this man he was no friend of Caesar’s, and the emperor would hear of it. That broke him. The chief priests cried that they had no king but Caesar. Pilate called for a basin, washed his hands before the crowd, and declared himself innocent of this man’s blood. Barabbas went free.
ch20.b077: At about that hour one of David’s messengers came panting up the stairs to the upper room of Nicodemus’s house. All through the morning they had been coming, one after another, each with a little more. This one brought the rest of it: the scourging, the crown of thorns, Barabbas, the governor washing his hands in a basin before the crowd. And then the last of it. The cross.
ch20.b078: Andrew closed his eyes. Peter, in his corner, could not lift his head. He heard every word. When the messenger spoke of the basin, Peter saw another basin: the one in the upper room the night before, and the Master kneeling with it before him. Peter had refused at first to let him wash his feet, and then, in his usual way, had begged to be washed all over. With water the Master had washed the feet of the twelve; with water, this morning, the governor had washed his own hands of him. Peter could not count how few hours lay between the two basins.
ch20.b079: And when he heard that the Master had stood before the crowd crowned with thorns, he remembered the face that had turned toward him under the torches a few hours before. That face was covered in blood now. And yet he knew the look in those eyes would not have changed. The eyes that looked down on the crowd and the eyes that had turned to him on the porch would be the same eyes. The thought hurt him all the more. And at the same time, very slightly, it held him up.
ch20.b080: From the courtyard of the praetorium the soldiers led the Master out toward Golgotha. Not one of the eleven walked behind him. His friends were in hiding, and John, the only one who had stayed beside him through the night, was out on the road to Bethany, running to fetch his mother.
ch20.b082: The course of events follows Papers 183–185. The palace of Annas and why John was known to its servants (184:0.1–0.3); the questioning by Annas and the steward’s blow (184:1.1–1.9); Judas coming to the gate of Annas and turning away, Peter throwing away his sword and being admitted at John’s request, the denials at the charcoal fire and on the porch, the cockcrow, the Master’s look, Peter weeping by the roadside, and his thinking he had cleverly evaded the servants (184:2.1–2.13); Peter returning to the camp at daybreak and being sent with David’s messenger to Andrew at the home of Nicodemus, and the places where the apostles hid (183:4.3–4.5); the court at Caiaphas’s palace, the false witnesses, the Master’s answer and the abuse, his sending John out, and the second session (184:3.1–5.11); and the trial before Pilate with John’s testimony, Herod, Barabbas, Claudia’s note, the scourging and the crown of thorns, Caiaphas’s threat, and the washing of hands (185:0.1–8.2). The Master sent John to fetch his mother as he was being taken to Herod (186:0.1), so John is not present for the later part of the trial; only enemies of Jesus witnessed it (185:6.1), and Jesus went out to Golgotha with no friend beside him (186:4.1). David’s messengers reported to the apostles about every half hour (186:3.3). John’s supplying the hiding apostles with news through the messengers comes from 183:4.5. Peter’s warning in the upper room is from 181:2.27–2.29.
ch20.b083: Character details come from Paper 139: Peter brave against frontal attack but shrinking before ridicule (139:2.6); his thinking, in the dark days after the denial, of the lesson of forgiving seventy times and seven (139:2.5; the question itself is at 159:1.4); Andrew’s sympathetic guidance of his brother (139:2.10); and Peter’s not fully believing in his forgiveness until after the resurrection (184:2.13). Peter’s pledge and the fire in the garden on the night of the ordination (140:6) carry over from Chapter 4.
ch20.b084: Added as fiction are the inner thoughts and memories of Peter and John; sensory details such as the smell of the charcoal and the sound of the cock; the portress’s first question rendered as spoken dialogue; Andrew receiving his brother at Nicodemus’s house; the messenger bringing news to that room; and Peter’s thought of the two basins (his reluctance at the foot washing is from 139:2.6). The denials are told in the order of the text without fixing their number.
ch20.b085: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
